The key enforcement happens at priority 6 with TokenAbsentChallengeRule, which issues a Challenge action whenever a request lacks a valid AWS WAF token — meaning any browser without a completed challenge/CAPTCHA response gets flagged by this missing-token label, triggering the challenge flow and an HTTP 202 response.

A browser silently solves this via JavaScript and retries successfully, but a non-browser client — like a server-to-server partner integration with no JS engine — can never solve the challenge, so it perpetually lacks the token and gets challenged on every request. This explains why the client sees seemingly "empty" responses: it's receiving a 202 challenge interstitial instead of real API data. And since Challenge returns a 2xx (202) rather than a 4xx status, the error-rate graphs stay flat even though the requests are effectively failing.

I want to confirm this theory by checking WAF metrics and sampled requests during the incident window (18:30-19:00 UTC, 2026-10-10) to verify the TokenAbsentChallengeRule was actively triggering challenges against the partner's traffic, pulling CloudWatch metrics like CountedRequests, BlockedRequests, and AllowedRequests under the AWS/WAFV2 namespace.
